newsitem.title: USA: Clinton solidifies lead as candidates hit Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Clinton solidifies lead as candidates hit Midwest.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole courted Midwestern voters on Monday as polls showed Clinton padding his already substantial lead with two weeks of campaigning left.
A confident Clinton did not even mention Dole by name and ignored Dole's attacks on foreign fundraisers collecting money for the Democratic Party from Asian businessmen.
He left the return fire to subordinates like Press Secretary Mike McCurry, who dismissed Dole's campaign finance attacks disdainfully as "a political deathbed conversion."
In a speech in Cleveland, Clinton focused on his efforts to help young people gain access to higher education by making it easier for them to gain student loans.

The latest Reuters daily tracking poll gave him a lead of nearly 11 percentage points over Dole at about 47 percent to 36 percent, with about 5 percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and nearly 11 percent undecided.
That meant a drop in the undecided bloc, most of which has been breaking for Clinton. Election day is November 5.
In another striking sign of Clinton's dominance, a new poll in the staunchly Republican tobacco-growing state of North Carolina showed the president leading Dole by 49 percent to 40 percent.
If Clinton can carry states like North Carolina, he might be looking at a landslide of historic proportions.
Dole, striving to reverse the poll numbers, attacked Clinton at a stopover in Detroit for an economic forum with Republican governors.

"President Clinton ... he's a real talker," Dole said, charging that Clinton was taking credit for millions of new jobs he did not create. "He goes right past the facts, the facts never get in the way."

But at his next rally in the Michigan town of Chelsea, in a Republican part of the state, Dole was faced with a number of pro-Clinton signs in the crowd and one person held up a sign in which Dole's 15 percent tax cut slogan had been altered to read "15 percent behind." The local high school band played the theme from "Mission Impossible."
Many Republicans have reportedly concluded the White House race is lost and are focusing on the fight to hold the party's majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.

A cluster of other poll results showed the depth of Dole's plight. Clinton led by 23 points in a Newsweek survey, 12 points according to ABC, 21 points in a CNN/USA Today poll, 18 in a Harris poll and 15 in the Hotline political newsletter.

In a speech on Sunday Dole tried to exploit reports that the Democrats and Clinton profited from fundraising by foreign business interests by proposing that only Americans eligible to vote be able to give money to candidates.

His campaign released another statement on Monday alleging that one Democratic fundraiser, John Huang, was the conduit for up to $5 million "in questionable and illegal campaign contributions," mostly from Asian companies.
The Democratic Party suspended Huang and returned some of the money he raised.
But Clinton campaign officials said Dole opposed campaign finance reform throughout his 35 years in Congress and had himself accepted donations from non-Americans.
"His conversion to the cause of campaign finance reform this late in the game is simply a political deathbed conversion," McCurry told reporters in Parma, Ohio, where Clinton was stumping.
The Clinton campaign began producing commercials that accused Dole and his party of taking more than $2 million from foreign contributors, including oil and tobacco firms.

The Clinton team also began running an ad designed to undercut Dole's effort to sow doubts about Clinton's character. In it Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter, Polly, was kidnapped and slain in California several years ago, credits Clinton with courage for pushing a tough anti-crime bill.
